The Convolution Theorem is a fundamental principle in signal processing and Fourier analysis. It states that under suitable conditions, the Fourier transform of the convolution of two functions is equal to the product of their Fourier transforms.

children.value: \mathcal{F}^{-1}\{ F(\omega) G(\omega) \} = f(t) * g(t) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(\tau) g(t - \tau) \, d\tau
children.html: F−1{F(ω)G(ω)}=f(t)∗g(t)=∫−∞∞f(τ)g(t−τ) dτ\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{ F(\omega) G(\omega) \} = f(t) * g(t) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(\tau) g(t - \tau) \, d\tauF−1{F(ω)G(ω)}=f(t)∗g(t)=∫−∞∞​f(τ)g(t−τ)dτ

children.value: This theorem provides a powerful link between operations in the time domain and the frequency domain:
Convolution in the time domain corresponds to multiplication in the frequency domain.
Multiplication in the time domain corresponds to convolution in the frequency domain.
